lines.text: From painted caves in Patagonia to the dance halls of Buenos Aires and the World Cup, this is the story of Argentina, a land of passion and upheaval.
Thousands of years ago, hunters in Patagonia pressed their hands to a cave wall and blew paint around them. The Cave of Hands still holds them.
In 1536 the Spanish founded Buenos Aires on the Rio de la Plata. It was abandoned, then refounded, and grew into a great port city.
By 1776 Buenos Aires was the capital of a Spanish viceroyalty, ruling a vast stretch of southern South America.
Soon after, Jose de San Martin was born. He would lead an army over the Andes to free Chile, and become Argentina's great hero.
In a single week of May 1810, the people of Buenos Aires replaced the Spanish viceroy with a government of their own.
Six years later a new nation stood at the southern tip of the continent: Argentina.
On the ninth of July 1816, in Tucuman, its leaders declared independence from Spain.
From the 1850s, millions of Italians and Spaniards crossed the ocean to farm the Pampas, and Argentina grew rich.
But there was a darker side. In the 1870s and 1880s the army seized Patagonia from its native peoples.
Meanwhile, in the port districts of Buenos Aires, a new music and dance was born, mixing African, European and local roots. The tango.
Carlos Gardel would carry the tango's song to the world in the twenties and thirties, before dying in a plane crash.
Juan Peron, an army officer, would be elected president in 1946, and his movement would shape Argentine politics for generations.
In 1897 climbers first reached the top of Aconcagua, the highest mountain anywhere outside Asia.
Jorge Luis Borges was born two years later. His stories of labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries made him one of the great writers of the century.
In 1905 Boca Juniors was founded in the port district of La Boca. Its matches against River Plate became legendary.
Eva Peron rose from actress to First Lady. She helped women win the vote, and the working people adored her. She died at just thirty-three.
Che Guevara, a young Argentine doctor, would join Fidel Castro's revolution in Cuba, and die trying to spark another in Bolivia.
In 1934 Argentina protected its side of the Iguazu Falls, a chain of waterfalls in forest full of jaguars and toucans.
Born in Buenos Aires in 1936, Jorge Bergoglio would become Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas.
From the mid seventies, a military regime waged a campaign of terror on its own people. Some thirty thousand disappeared.
In a poor district of Buenos Aires, Diego Maradona was born. He would captain Argentina to the 1986 World Cup.
Javier Milei, a libertarian economist, would be elected president in 2023.
In 1977, mothers of the disappeared began marching every week in the Plaza de Mayo, demanding to know what had happened to their children.
The next year Argentina hosted the World Cup under the junta, and won it, with two goals from Mario Kempes in the final.
In 1982 the junta occupied the Falkland Islands. British forces took them back within months, and the military government fell soon after.
In Rosario, in 1987, Lionel Messi was born. He would grow into one of the greatest footballers of all time.
In 1994 a bomb destroyed a Jewish centre in Buenos Aires, killing eighty-five people.
By the late nineties the economy was sinking. Argentina defaulted on its debts and cut the peso loose from the dollar.
In December 2001, banks froze people's savings, riots filled the streets, and the government fell.
And in Qatar in 2022, Messi led Argentina to beat France on penalties, the country's third World Cup.
Through dictatorship and crisis, tango and football, Argentina keeps its fierce and restless spirit.
